Today's date is the 16th of January.

Okay, this is tape one, Leroy "Slam" Stewart, Smithsonian Institute Jazz Oral History Orchestra Program. Well, Mr. Stewart, the first thing I would like to ask you is when and where you were born and what you know about your family background, if you have like, say, Indian, Scotch, Irish, Canadian, whatever.
The answer -- well, first of all, I was born in Englewood, New Jersey, and that happened September 21st, 1914. So that kind of puts me up there, don't you think?
A little bit, yeah.

And, of course, my parents -- I was the only child, and my parents brought me up sort of strict-like. I went to school. I finished high school, of course. During high school years and before I was very interested in music, and as a matter of fact, before I even went to high school, I -- this goes back to the age of around seven years old.

My folks bought me a little violin, and, of course, I used to listen to the big bands on the radio. That was before -- long before TV came in. And I heard some pretty good sounds. Music so interested me, and I was sort of interested in music, listening to the big bands that used to broadcast in

Philadelphia and New York, you know, and Northwest sometimes, and I was able to listen to especially Duke Ellington and -- there were quite a few -- Jimmie Lunceford. And it sort of was -- I was very interested -- the sound really knocked me out, you know.
When you were -- what kind of a neighborhood did you grow up in?

Well, a small town, Englewood, right across from New York, you might say. I was brought up in a very country, you know, it was real country out there, and the neighborhood kids -- it was a very nice neighborhood, and of course I friends beautiful, had lots of things. And as I was going along in years and studying the violin, I had a violin teacher whose name was -- I will never forget his name. His name - We used to call him Professor Scott, and he -- he taught me some good things about the fiddle, and I learned pretty good. But I don't -- even until today I don't think I learned too well, because I wasn't really interested in the little violin, especially when I used to listen to the big bands and what have you. Something sort of hit me when I was listening, and I'm sure even up until today that that was the old bass fiddle that the fellows -- the fellow in -- the bassiest in the band was playing, and the sound, it really sounded so good to me that the violin, I didn't even half study it, you know. That's probably the reason why I switched to the bass
fiddle.
What kind of occupation was your family involved in?

Well, my dad was a sort of a caretaker, gardener and what have you. He worked for -- he used to cut grass and garden -- garden for the folks up on the hill, you know. That was his job. One person that he worked for in gardening and what have you was Dwight Morrow. You probably heard of the Morrow family from Englewood. And their daughter was Anne Morrow. She married Charles Lindbergh. And that was quite a gig there working for them, because it was a way of living, you know, means of living, and we got along very well.
What did he think about them? Did he ever talk to you about the family?

Yes. They were wonderful people. They did wonderful things for us. You know -- they -- for my family they were very wonderful. Of course, I didn't see too much of them because they were more or less travelers and big timers, you might say, in politics and all that.
When you say they did wonderful things for the family, like what?
Well, speaking of us, you mean?
Yeah.
They were very interested in my music.

And somehow they -- they had a lot to do with my financing my career in music later on. As a matter of fact, I'm sure that they were a big help to my family in sending me to music school in Boston -- in Boston when I got out of high school. I'm sure that they were a big help in my music, you know, the financial part.
They sent me away to Boston to study the bass. That's when I forgot all the little -- forgot about the little violin. I used to call it the squeak box.
(Laughter.)
I didn't like it too much, you know.
And I was so interested in the bass fiddle. So that it wound up that my folks sent me up to Boston to try to make a career in music, especially playing the bass fiddle.
What was the -- I was talking with Sonny Greer. He grew up in Long Branch, New Jersey.
Oh, yes.

And he told me that -- that one of the things was that he said in Long Branch there was like -- there wasn't any like segregation in an overt sense like a white and a black school. He said there was a certain -- there were certain kinds of racial restrictions, but by and large he more or less, you know, he and everybody else kind of -- everybody was kind of -- it was kind of a mixed neighborhood. So how was - what kind of neighborhood was yours?
Yeah, that's right, come to think of it.

That's about the way it was around home in Englewood. There wasn't really any segregation. What I mean, I didn't notice it, and especially at that age I was just like all of the fellows, you know, and girls in school. You know what I mean.
I played a little bit of basketball and what have you -- and we were just all like one another, you know.

When did you become aware of the fact that there was any social differences in terms of the treatment of people, Negroes as opposed to whites? Did you become aware of that in Englewood or after you left home?
I became aware of that more or less when I left home.
When you went to Boston?

When I went to Boston, yes. Then at the -- a few things that happened, you know, even that I hadn't read about, you know, or heard about segregation and what have you, and that's when I started to see some of those things happen, you know.
Even at that time when I went to Boston by train, and even at that time. I noticed some things on the train going up even
Like what?

Like the color of the parlor cars and what -- they had little restrictions, you know. Even the restroom facilities, what have you -- at times I did notice that they did have a place for colored, a place for white, you know, that, and, of course, even when I went to Boston restaurants
and railroad stations, you know, they had a bit of segregation there at that point.

Now, when you were -- like in this program here, in this tribute to Erroll Garner that you did in March of 1978, there's a photograph of you in the high school orchestra in New Jersey, in Englewood, New Jersey. And in the photograph there's like this one, two, there are three -- three colored people, and one of them was you, playing with the bass. The guy holding the drum -- there's another guy sitting behind the saxophones.
Right.
Now, what -- you were playing the bass by then.

I was playing the bass, at least trying to. I didn't know one note from the other, but I had a pretty good ear, you know, and I managed to get by. One of the fiddle players in the school orchestra, he had to show me how to even tune the bass, which is altogether reverse from the little violin, which -- I had studied, you know, but I didn't know exactly how the bass was supposed to be tuned.
Well, you -- now, you were playing the -- you began playing the violin when you were seven, you said.
Yes, right.
So now, when did you switch over to the bass?
Oh, I switched over, I'd say, when I was about 14.
14. So you played the violin for about seven years before you --
Sure, yes.
-- before you started playing the bass.
Right.
And so you began to become interested in the bass from radio broadcasts.
That's right. Yes.
Now, did many bands -- did many or any bands perform in Englewood at that time?

No, there weren't any bands performing in Englewood. I find that, when I started playing the bass fiddle, I used to -- oh, let's see, I was about at least -- oh, 15, 16, or possibly 17, I'd say. I used to travel to other towns like Newark, and I joined a little jazz combo. And by that time I was real, real hot and heavy and playing by ear, you know. And I joined this combo. They had heard about me.

So at that time Dad had given me a little car, and I was able to get around, you know, and I was, oh, traveling doing one nighters once in a while, as far as Newark, and Passaic and around -- let's see. The name of this outfit was called Sonny Marshall and his Harlem Stompers. It's something like that. It was a small combo, you know, five, six pieces.
What, did you play for dances? You played for dances?
Played for dances.
Were these like adult dances or for teenage dances?
Well, it was adults, you know. And that was really the start of my trying to do something with the bass.

Now, when you were playing, were you playing -- when you were playing these jobs in Sonny Marshall's band, do you remember who -- what the other instrumentalists were, who they were, what instruments they played?

Right now it's going to be hard for me to remember. Oh, we had trombone. Trombone Red they used to call him. I forget his last name. And a drummer -- and Sonny Marshall, he played the alto sax. And we had a piano player, and I've forgotten some of the names of fellows, but that was really the start of my getting a little bit of experience, playing what you might say in a small combo, jazz or what you might say.

What kind of -- did you all have any -- any particular bands that you were emulating at that time. Who were they -- you know, what records -- were you all listening to records, modeling what you were doing off -- from records that were around, from radio broadcasts, or did Marshall himself have

own
records on book?
No, listening to radio and a couple of records that my folks had gotten for me, you know.
Do you remember whose recordings you listened to?

Yeah. Duke Ellington especially. And I remember first time that I saw Duke Ellington and his band in person, my folks took me over to the Apollo Theater at 125th Street in New York to see him. He was appearing there.
How old were you then, about?
I was around, oh, 19, somewhere.
So this was near 1930? You were born in 1914 --
Yes.
-- no, that would be somewhere after --
About '33, something like that.
Who was playing bass with the band?
Oh, gee -- what was his name?
Wellman Braud, was it Wellman Braud?
No. Braud wasn't -- the name was Green -- Greenstreet -- Green -- I forget his name. I don't think Wellman Braud was playing with him. "Bro," I think how you think how you propounce that.
You know, Sonny Greer says "Bro," so maybe that's what it was.
Braud, Wellman, yes.
Maybe it was --
It may have been Wellman Braud. But anyway, I will never forget that first visit, you know, the folks taking me over to see the band at the Apollo.
And so like what kind -- do you remember . So you were really impressed by the band.
Yes, I was.
Could you hear the bass well?
Yes, I did.
Now, were they --
That was my main -- my main interest there, the bass fiddler.
Uh-huh. Was -- at that time was the bass -- did they use amplification for the bass of any sort, the bass player?

No, they probably had mikes -- a mike nearby so he could be heard. I heard the whole -- they probably had several mikes on the stage, you know, so it would pick up just about anything and everything.

That was my main interest, was the bass fiddle.

But now, you -- when you were working in this band with Sonny Marshall, and you were playing around at these dances and stuff, did you -- do you remember what kind of repertoire you all -- you all had, what tunes, what some of the tunes were you were playing, like standards or originals (unintelligible)

Oh, a lot of blues and -- and, of course, you know, like "Shine" maybe. I don't know -- a lot of tunes that I can't remember of that time. It's hard to remember right now. But I kept up with them, sure, whatever they did. "Chinatown, My Chinatown," "Charleston," and I can't remember some of those things. It's really weird.
Well, that's a long time. I just wanted, you know, general -- did you -- how many key -- did you all play in many keys or did you play on (inaudible)?
They played -- yes, we played in maybe at least three keys, standard, you know, C --
B flat and F?
B flat, and then F, yeah, mostly, you know.
Now, when you -- so now, when did you move to New York. You stayed --
Well --
Oh, excuse me. You were -- now, when did you -- you started studying in Boston after --
In Boston --
-- after you graduated from high school.
Yes. That was around 1934.
That you went to Boston?
I went to Boston, yes.
Now, you had -- you had been working
mostly with Sonny Marshall's band --
That's right.
-- at that time.
Yes.

Now, what -- did -- were there any particular people that you modeled yourself on in your early years of playing the bass? Because now -- because this is the reason I ask you. Sonny Greer told me that the first time that was in New York he the first time that the guys heard a string bass was in Jean Gene Bollette's band. Before that everybody played tuba.
Oh, yes.

And when they heard -- when Wellman Braud saw that, he said he was through with the tuba. He had had the bass, and he started playing the bass. So what I was trying to get at was, you know, like young trumpet players, say, might have been listening to Jabbo Smith or --
Jabbo.

-- King Oliver, Louis Armstrong or something, and I was wondering who you as a bassist were listening to or whether any guys were there that impressed you to where you emulated what they played or that you tried to figure out what they were playing.
Well, when I first went to Boston, I think it went this way. I was studying at the same time and got in Boston a gig at a place called the Little Dixie. And there was a band I

there by the name of Dean Earl and his -- I forget what they called it. Dean Earl had the band at the time. And in the band was a trumpet player by name of Jabbo Jenkins, and drummer, I forget what his name was. But also I remember the saxophonist, alto saxophone player doubled on a little violin. His name was Ray Perry.
Ray Perry.
Ray Perry, yeah. Perry it was. And, of course, who else did they have. The guitar player, I can't remember his name. But that's the way I really had quite an experience in playing with this group.
Oh, went to well, you worked in that band.

Yes, I went to the band, and that lasted a little while. It was very good for me. As a matter of fact, that's where I got my style of playing the bass the way I play it. I learned how to do it from the experience I had, especially playing with Ray Perry, especially when he was playing his violin. That's where I got the idea of playing the bass idea, sawing the bass and humming along with it, because that's what he used to do. He used to sing along with his violin, right in the same register as when he was playing his solos and what have you.

I don't see how in the world he could do that because his violin being so high, but he put his voice right up there with his violin. And so that kind of struck me -- it kind of hit me some kind of way where I said I have to do it on the bass
fiddle you, know, hum along with it. And that's the way I started humming along with my bass fiddle.
That's when you began that part.
That's right, yeah.

That's not -- yeah, but that's not exactly what I meant, the question. I meant -- when you had mentioned started, before you developed what became known for, when you first started playing, do you remember what bass players you were listening to?
Oh, yes. Well, (inaudible), of course, and, oh, let's see. There's another bass player. I forget his name. He used to be with Cab Calloway. Green -- Green something. (Al Morgan)
Yeah, we can look his name up. We've got those records books in there, big --
Yes, that's right.
-- bands.
He kind of was fascinating. He played good, and he used to dance around with his bass, you know. He used to -- while he was plucking his bass, used to he hop around --
Oh, he would turn all the way around in a circle while he played?
Turned all the way around in a circle, yeah. That's what fascinated me even more so.
He would be playing --
Playing --
-- the bass as he --
And dancing right around with it.
Oh, that's -- that's pretty --
And that was real --
(Inaudible).
(Inaudible) Bullmoose?
(Interruption.)
So now, when you first started playing the bass, with the bass, what were the bass players playing? Were they playing syncopated figures, or were they walking?
Well, it was more or less walking.
When you began?
Well, yeah. I started out just playing straight bass and pizzicato, plucking, you know.
Because from all the things I've heard, guys would be playing figures like boom, boom, boom, boom-boom-boom-boom, you know, like kind of --
Yeah.
-- rather than like, rather than, say, doon, tuck-a, doon, doon, doon.
They weren't doing that then. No, not at all.
They weren't playing that then. It was like --
A little bit of syncopation here and there, you know, but just more or less straight -- straight, good bass, of course. And oh this fellow -- oh, I forget the --
The Calloway bass player?
Yeah.
(Interruption.)
So now, in those days, you say, you're saying the bass players were playing, they were playing more like syncopated figures more like -- more like tuba?
Yes. Just like you say, duh, duh, duh, duh, duh, doon-doon-doon-doon, doo, doo, doo, straight more or less, straight bass.
Now, where did you study when you were in Boston?

I studied at a little place called the Boston Conservatory of Music. It was a small place, conservatory over -- it was located over Child's Restaurant, on the second floor. It was a rather small place on the corner of Massachusetts and Columbus Avenue.
And who were your teachers? Remember your teachers?
Oh, I remember one -- the only teacher that I had for the short time that I studied with him, his name was Al Ropes.
Ropes?
Ropes, R-o-p-e-s.
Uh-huh. And what did you study from him?

I studied how to use the bow, and, of course, I had a bit of solfeggio and I -- he really gave me the fundamentals, like the notes and the, you know, solfeggio, beats and what have you. Reading. He really helped me to, how to read, which I'm very thankful for, you know, being able to read, you know, because there are times when that really is a big help.
Well now, you didn't -- those seven years that you studied the violin, you didn't learn notation or sight reading in those years?
Oh, yes.
But you, oh, that's right. That's another clef, though.
In another clef.
Right, violin, right. So you went to study at the Boston Conservatory. That's when you learned how to read the bass clef.
That's right, yeah.
But now, when you were -- were you -- how were you making it when you were in the orchestra in high school? Was there much reading for you to do?
I didn't do any reading there at all. I just went on my ear. You should have seen me back there when they had assembly, I was -- when they played the marches,
I listened real good, and somehow I just hit the right notes. I found the notes — on my bass. And I played by ear.
Now, did the teacher who was over the orchestra know that you were playing by ear?
Yeah, she knew it.
(Laughter.)

It was a lady teacher. I never will forget her, her name, Margaret Reed, and we had a beautiful time there. It didn't make any difference to her whether I could read or not, you know. We happened to have -- when I changed over to the bass fiddle, I used to play a little violin too in the orchestra, but I changed over real quick.

They had a, happened to have a bass fiddle in the orchestra rooms, which I became very interested in, and I asked her, could I use it, you know, could I try it out. And she said, go ahead. And like I say, right there one of the fiddle players showed me how to tune, because it's the reverse from the little violin.
Now, the bass is tuned in fourths, right?
In fourths, yes.
Now, what is the violin tuned in?
In fifths.
The violin's tuned in fifths, right.
Yeah. Okay, yeah. So that's a different story.
Like E, A, D, G, going down, you know, on violin, whereas G, D, A, E on the bass, going down.
Uh-huh, right. Right. Now, so then what kind of material were you playing in school orchestra?
Oh, just the marches, you know.
Sousa and stuff like that?
That's right, da, da-da-da-da, da, da, pah, dee-pah-dah-dey-dah, buh, buh, you know, all that.
Yeah. And were you playing pizzicato, or were you bowing?
Pizzicato.
Pizzicato. Now, were you amplified in the school orchestra?
No.
There was no amplification?
I was just standing back there, plucking away, you know.
Now, did you all play any performances for people other than the students?

No, I don't remember. We probably had a couple of times when we played for maybe where the parents came in for assembly or a play of some sort, you know, school play, but that was -- I can't quite remember.
Now, did your parents ever come to hear you? Do you remember whether they came to hear you while you
Yes, they did.
They did.
Yes. Yes.
How did they -- were they proud of you?
Oh, they were very, very proud, yes.
Now, were your grandparents in Englewood or where were they?

No, like I said, I was the only kid, and as far as I know, I never will today quite remember whether it was true or not, but I was told that I was an adopted kid, you know. Of course, it makes no difference to me, you know. And, of course --
You were told by whom, by your parents or by somebody outside the family?

Outside, which come to think of it, I probably was because by my birth certificate I was under a different name, come to think of it, but that didn't make a difference. As far as my parents were concerned, that was the real thing for me, you know. They raised me. I will never forget and appreciate the way they raised me. They really had -- you might say they made something out of me, you know, helped me to make something out of myself, you know.
Now, you say you had a very disciplined, very strict kind of --
Very strict, yes, right.
You learned that, like you had chores you were supposed to do?
The chores and, of course, I -- they didn't have to make me, but I was used to going to church, you know, and I sang in the choir. And I did.
What did you say you sang? You sang alto?
No, I sang baritone-like.
Oh, you sang baritone? That's funny because from hearing you sing with the bass, I would have thought you sang alto.

No. With the bass it's a different octave above when I'm playing thing, especially when I'm singing and (inaudible) the bow, which I'd like to get into the reason why I got into this, on account of --
The violin.
-- the violin, the violin's sight -Ray Perry. And we happened to be working in the same group, Dean Earl --
Right.
-- his orchestra. And we played in this nightclub, and the Little Dixie, it was called. And that's where I got the idea to hum along with my bass fiddle.
Now, when you were -- getting back to --

I'm trying to get some -- fill in a few things, as much background, early, as -- you didn't have, when your family became aware of the fact that you were going to become a musician, were -- they didn't try to discourage you or anything?
No, they didn't. In fact, they encouraged me. And that's like when I wanted to go away to study, they were all for it, you know. And that's how I wound up in -- at the Conservatory in Boston.
Now, did you -- did you meet other wings of your family other than your mother and father? Were any of them musically inclined or --
No. Come to think of it, none of them -- my so called cousins, what have you, uncle, what have you.
None of them were musicians?
No, only one.
Did they all live in New Jersey?
Yeah.
So you didn't have any -- you didn't have any -- did you ever have any contact with any members of your family in the South or Midwest or anything like that?
No.
No, it was all there?
Right there in Englewood, yes.
Englewood of thereabouts?
Thereabouts, yes.
Now, when you were -- so now, you really learned how to read for the bass in the Conservatory, as you said. Now, how long did you study there?

I didn't study too long. I'd say about half of a semester. As a matter of fact, I -- most of my experience in reading after I got a good foundation, was in nightclubs and traveling around and what have you in the years later on.
Now, why did you only stay there a half of a term?

Well, because, for one thing, I wasn't making quite enough money at that time in order to keep up my -- my folks sent me there and paid for a half term, you know, tuition for the half term, and after that I just didn't have probably enough to continue, which I don't exactly regret. But at times I thought maybe if I could have stayed, I may have learned a little bit more to my advantage, you know.

But as I say -- as I say, most of my experience is from -- is working in these groups and what have you and traveling and still learning how to maneuver the bass fiddle.
Now, when you left, you left the Boston Conservatory, what did you begin? What did you do after you left?
Well, I got a call from a fellow in Buffalo who had a band at a club in Buffalo. He was passing

through Boston while I was there, and he said he liked the way I played, you know, and said that, if he ever needed a bass player, he's going to call on me, you know, and I would be coming that way or going back home. I told him I was going back home very soon after that time, but maybe I would stop on the way going home and pay him a visit, or something like that. But before that he had given me a call, and it came at a very opportune time. So I went to Buffalo and joined him, and that was Peanuts Holland.
And he had a little group at a club there in Buffalo which I joined. That was in 1935.
So 1935, you were 21 then?
Yeah.
And how long did you stay with that band?
I stayed there about, oh, maybe a half a year, something like that.
What style band was it, what kind of repertoire did you play?
It's jam -- jazz-like, you know. They had very, quite a repertoire. All the modern numbers of that time, you know.
Like 'Mood Indigo.'?
Oh, yes, right.
'Sophisticated Lady.'?
That's right.
Let's see what else?
It wasn't --
"King Porter Stomp", did you play that?
"The A Train," didn't that come along?
"A Train" went to about '40. That was Strayhorn was with the band.
That's around '40. That's right. But the numbers during -- this was the mid-'30s.
"Sweet Georgia Brown"?
That's right, "Sweet Georgia Brown."
"Sweet Georgia Brown" and "I've Got Rhythm."
"I've Got Rhythm", right.
Let's see, "Mood Indigo."
Yeah. Wasn't "I'm in the Mood for Love?"
It was probably around, it was around in there.
It was around in there.
Yeah, so now were they like what --
(Side B.)
-- in the band for about six months?
I'd say that, yes.
And you played, where did you play, mostly in Buffalo or did you travel around?
I played one place in Buffalo. The name of the place was called the Silver Grill.
The Silver Grill?
At that time it was a little restaurant, nightclub, like --
How many sets did you play in those days?
Oh, let's see. We started, I'd say, around maybe 8:30 or 9:00 o'clock and ended up around 1:00, something like that.
Were you playing 20-40 then, or 40-20?
I think so, yes.
40 minutes on, 20 minutes off.
That's right. Yes, come to of it, think it was.
Okay, all right. Now, in that band were they playing, Peanuts Holland, who did he like? Who were his idols that he taught you about, the guys that really liked he -- what did he play, by the way?
He played trumpet.
He was a trumpeter.
He was quite a trumpeter, yes.
Who did he like? Did he like Louis Armstrong or --
Oh, yes, Louis and quite a few of the trumpet players coming up at that time.
Like Rex Stewart.
Rex, right.
Cootie Williams?
Cootie.
Walter Page?
Walter Page?
I mean Hot Lips Page.
Hot Lips, oh, yes, Hot Lips.
Right, Hot Lips Page, yeah.
Well, it's real surprising. There were quite a few trumpeters that came around during those years.
Were you -- were the things that you had to play in the band, did they have written charts for you or did you -- were you still playing by ear?
Still playing by ear, yes.
Were they, was this band too only playing like for two or three keys like C and B flat and F?
That's right.
They were basically in those three keys?
Basically, yes.
Okay. Now, were there any people in that band who later became well known players, in this Peanuts Holland band?
Not that I -- I don't quite remember. I know Peanuts, that years later he played with Count Basie and what have you. But as far as the other members, the saxophone
x no. Charlie Barnet, Don Redman. Cob Collogay's small band

player, alto sax, his name was Don Stovall, and, of course, as the years went on by, you lose track of these fellows. But Peanuts, he was quite a trumpeter, and you heard more about him as the years went by. And I hadn't even left the band to venture further, further near home, that is.
Who owned the Silver Grill? I mean, was it -- what kind of a place was it?
It was -- I forget the manager's name. So long ago, of course, you know.
Was this, was it a -- was this a Negro club or white club?
No, white club.
It was a white club.
Yeah. It was owned by whites.
And the clientele?
The clientele was mixed.
Oh, it was a mixed clientele?
Oh, sure, yes.
And there was no -- there were no problems?
No problems.
Oh, that's very unusual in 1935.
That's right, yeah.
And this was in Buffalo?
In Buffalo, yeah.
There was no -- you didn't have any problem with fraternizing with the --

Did he ever talk to you about any musicians that he was impressed with from his home town?

Well, no, not really. Of course, he was from a musical family, and if I'm not mistaken, I think one of his brothers played piano also, and he was from a musical family and all -- I guess that was about it. Most of our interest was music, yeah. I don't think he was interested in sports at all.
Huh. What about movies. Did you guys go to movies much in those days?

Well, I went to movies once in a while, probably not as much as a lot of people do. But to the movies -- I went quite a bit, come to think of it, until later on when TV came out. Then -- I haven't been in a theater, I might
say, in the last 20 years to see a movie, really, actually to see a movie.
So you just -- you did go see a lot of films in those days?
Not too many, just enough to pass the time when I wasn't working on that bass fiddle, you know.
How did you -- how did you come about making the movie that you're in now with Slim Gaillard?

Well, Slim and I, as I mentioned before, when we left New York, the first place that we hit was Los Angeles. And we were -- while we were working a couple of the clubs out there, we were approached to make this film or two that we made, and it just happened through our agent and, you know.
This guy, Martin Block?

Martin Block, no, he wasn't on the scene then. It was the William Morris agent. In fact, the William Morris agent bought Martin Block's contract, and they were handling Slim (Inaudible) and myself at that time. So the William Morris agency did quite a little, few things for us, nice things, of course, like a couple of movies we were in. So that's how that happened.
How -- were you all well paid for working in the movies?
Well, fairly, fairly good. Let's see.
HEMLOCK (Hellzapoppin')

That Hell's A'Poppin' that Slim and I made, if I remember, my salary was about $750.00 during those days, you know, just to do a little segment there. I didn't think that was too bad, you know. So that was about it.
How was it -- did you all meet many of the people in the cast of the movie you were working on, or did you just go in and do the scene?
Well, we managed to meet quite a few of the people in the movie, Olson and Johnson.
Martha Raye.
Martha Raye.
Mischa Auer, I think he was in there.
Yeah, and -- Hell's A'Poppin' -- let's see. I was just wondering, I was thinking about another picture that Slim wasn't with me that I made with Fats Waller.
Oh, which one was that?
That was called Ain't Misbehavin'. (viz. below)
Oh, you made -- that was a film!
The movie.
Was it a -- was it a short film, or was it --
It was a short.
A short. (Inaudible).
(Interruption.)
So actually the movie wasn't Ain't
It was Stormy Weather.
And you were -- you were in the -- let's see. I think there were two sequences that Waller was in.
I was in the one with Waller and I think Rex Stewart was in that. (No)
Now, there's a scene in there, I think, where Zutty Singleton is playing drums.
Zutty, he was on drums.
And there's some scene that takes place in this cafe or something.
Yeah.
And I think he -- yeah, I don't remember which song offhand he plays in there, but I think he does play 'Ain't Misbehavin'.'
Ain't Misbehavin'.
In that sequence -- did you know -- did you know Waller well?
Waller? Fairly well. That was around, that was the first time I have really met him.
Oh, was it in the movie?
Yeah.
How did -- what -- how did he strike you?
Oh, he was quite a fellow. He was comical. Even in real life he was a very wonderful person.
And I was so glad to get with him to play, you know, (inaudible) with him.
What did you think of his musicianship in comparison to, say—
Tremendous, yeah. He played that piano and organ, you know.
Did you play with him in any situations other than that movie?
Well, no, I think that was the only thing.
That's the only time you had a chance to play with him?
That's the only time I ever had a chance to play with him, yes.
Because he didn't -- like he died some months, not very long after that movie.
Not too long after that. And he was really young. I think he was around 48, like that, when he passed. [ed. - 39]
Yeah. He was young. Like what did -- I mean were you around that production as it was made? Were you, I mean were you around it much, or did you just go in and do that particular sequence?
Well, I just went in and did that particular segment of it. And I may have stayed around, oh,
for another portion of it. But I wasn't around too long.
What did you think of the movie, the movie industry, even though you weren't involved in it that much? How did it strike you?
Well, I didn't really think anything of it. It was just one of those things that I was even glad to even get into, you know.
Were you paid playing as well for Stormy Weather as you were for the Hell's A'Poppin' movie?
Just about, sure.
Did you -- so in that situation did you meet Lena Horne and --
Yes.
-- Bill Robinson?
That's right, oh, yes.
In that situation. And how did they come over?
They came over very,very well, sure.
They were -- you -- so they didn't have what you (inaudible). They (inaudible), so they were like, they came off to you as more or less down to earth kind of people.
Down to earth, yes.
(Inaudible) you didn't get into any --
Right.
-- static or anything.
No.
That's good. Now, when you -- did you ever work with Benny Carter in those days?
I sat in on a couple of after hour sessions with him in L.A., yes.
Oh, you met him in Los Angeles?
Yes, right.
What, during the time that you were making the movie?
During the time that I was out there with Slim.
Uh-huh.
Yes.
Was Carter living out there at that time or was he just there on a tour?
I think he was living there, yes.

He was there living. Now, when you came to Los Angeles, what were the circumstances under which musicians worked then, because I know that when in 1945, I think it was, '45 or '46, when Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie came out there, there -- the city, you know, the city was somewhat segregated. The club, I think it played -- I don't know. It was some club that played in Hollywood, had a backwards racial policy, if I remember. And most of the Black bands that came through Los Angeles at that time didn't -- I
think they tended to work on Central Avenue more often.

Central Avenue. Well, I actually didn't run across any situation like that. The couple of places that I worked even with Art Tatum at the Streets of Paris on Hollywood Boulevard, that was -- there was no segregation and like that. Everything was cool, right down to earth.
Uh-huh.
And, of course, when I worked the 331 Club with Slim and the Swanee Inn with Slim, those, all the clubs that I worked were mixed, and everything was great.
Now, where did you all live when you worked in Los Angeles?
Well, we lived in hotels.
I mean do you remember which hotels you stayed at?
And, of course, I had my own home out there.
Oh, you had a home out there?
Sure. Yes.
Had you bought it, you know, how did you --
No, it wasn't my own home. I just was renting -- a little bungalow.
Where? In what section of Los Angeles?
Oh, that wasn't far from Central Avenue on 41st Street, I think it was, if I remember correctly.
Now, did you keep, did you keep that place year around or did you just rent it for when you were in town?
Just while I was in town, yeah, "Auto-town" something like living in (inaudible) more or less.
Now, did you, what did you, how, the music scene at that time, what was it like in the Central Avenue situation then?
It was -- the music scene was great. I think you mentioned that Alabam, was it?
Club Alabam, yeah.

Club Alabam, I think that was about the only place on Central Avenue at that time, but then they had their after hour joints that we used to, musicians used to go after they finished work and Art Tatum and I and Tiny and a lot of musicians used to frequent this particular place. It was called Lovejoys, and it was quite an after hours spot. They used to call it Lovejoys, the "Home of the Big Legged Chicken," because he used to serve chicken, you know, and food after hours.
Do you remember where the place was?
I think it was on the corner of Central and Vermont.
Vernon. Vernon and Central.
Vernon Avenue, was it?
Something like that.
Boulevard.
Yeah, something like that. Yes, it wasn't very far from the Dunbar Hotel.
That's right, Dunbar Hotel.
Just a few blocks up the street.
That's right.
Now, a lot of the musicians then lived at the Dunbar.
That's right, yeah.
It's sort of like when -- now, who were some of the guys that you recall being on the scene in Los Angeles. You said like Benny Carter was there.
Yeah. Oh, gee. Now I really have to put my thinking cap on. Well, I met Lester Young out there for the first time.
Did you play with him?

Yes. In fact, after I came back East later on, I even recorded with Lester, made some beautiful recordings with him. I met him. And Lester had a brother who played drums. His name was Lee, Lee Young. I met him.
How did, what kind of a person was -- a lot of people described Lester Young as being a rather eccentric
No, he didn't. He didn't strike me that way. To me he used to keep to himself quite a bit, you know. He didn't have too much to do with anybody. What would you say that is, being real cool or --
Rather reserved.
Reserved, yes.
He wasn't like an exuberant kind of guy.
That's right. He wasn't that way at all and a wonderful fellow.
Under what circumstances did you meet him? Did you meet him --
At a session.
Was he playing?
Yeah.
He was playing. You all played together at that point.
Sure.
Had you -- that wasn't the first time that you heard him, was it?
No. That wasn't the first time.
How did he -- how did his playing -- what did you think of his playing when you first heard him?
It was -- to me it was quite different from the other, you might say, from Coleman Hawkins. He really
had -- just his style of blowing was real mellow. And the way he went about it, it was very enjoyable to me.

Well, what did you think of his -- what did you think of his harmonic ideas, how did, because, you know, sometimes, well, oftentimes really in Young's playing he'll like anticipate the harmony. You know, he'll play a chord before it falls and it -- and he'll play something, say it was a C7, a chord everybody in the world could play.
Yeah.
He might play that just before the piano player or the bassist strikes the chord. Did that -- did that stick out to you when he was --
Oh, yes. Yes, and he played beautiful changes as he went along, passing, you know, chords into one another. It was great. The sound was so beautiful.
Also he didn't -- because I know he had a lot of problems when he first started playing because his style was so unusual.
Yeah.
But it didn't -- it didn't --
I would never notice it myself.
It didn't bother --
No.
It didn't rub you the wrong way, so to speak. When you first heard it, you kind of liked it?
Yes.
Do you remember the circumstances under which you first heard him play? Did you hear him on record or radio broadcasts?

I heard him on record and, if I'm not mistaken, I saw him with Count Basie, and that was about it. That was about the first time, especially on records, you know. And when I met him -- when I first met him, it was a real thrill to me, you know, like a lot of the cats that I had heard on records. And when I finally met them, it was a big kick, you know.
Did he have a big sound?
Yes, he did.
He did, huh?
Yes, he did.
He had a big sound.
And quite different from all the other great tenor saxophone players, you know, beautiful --
Yeah, because, you know, I had thought that from the records, because some people had said that he had a small sound.

Yeah, well, that goes along the way some people think. Of course, you might say that in comparison to Coleman Hawkins' sound or even Ben Webster, you might say that his sound wasn't quite as big at times as Ben Webster's
sound or Coleman Hawkins' or Chu Berry and what have you. (inaudible). But most of the time his sound was pretty good.
Now, when you played with him, did you find him to be like a guy who improvised a lot or a guy who had a lot of pet phrases and stuff that he used?
Well, I didn't notice too much. I think he improvised more so than having a lot of -- more so than having a lot of pet phrases, you know. He could improvise mostly all the time.
When you played with him at this session the first time you got a chance to play with him, do you remember who some of the other guys were who played at that particular session?

Well, it's hard to say. I'm sure that Art Tatum was there. And at this one our guitarist, Everett Barksdale, he was on the scene, and I think Duke Ellington was in town with his band also, and Ray Nance was there, I remember, this particular session. And if I'm not mistaken Jimmy Blanton came in.
Oh, well, this was -- this was quite -- this was quite a session, yeah.
Yes, it was.
(Recording interrupted.)
So then at this session there were quite a few musicians of stature at this particular session?

That's for sure. As a matter of fact, on another occasion which wasn't -- that didn't take place at this particular session, but I'd like to mention that one of the sessions that we did have was out at a friend of ours' home. A young lady by the name of Mary Wilkinson gave a party for quite a few of the musicians, which included Nat King Cole, Jimmy Blanton and Art Tatum and myself and our guitarist and what have you, and we had quite a session at her home this afternoon it took place.

One thing that surprised me so very much was, in sitting in with Nat Cole, it was quite a thrill, you know, for me, that is, to be playing with Nat. And we were running through a couple of changes and this and that, the other. The lady of the house kind of intervened and asked Nat Cole to -- 'Why don't you sing, Nat?' And, of course, one word we went on after the other. As a matter of fact, it was kind of a surprise for her to ask him that, you know, because I'd never heard him sing before. And evidently she did.

So that was my first experience in hearing Nat Cole sing, and that was quite a thing. I was very surprised. And as you know yourself, even through the years Nat Cole, some people didn't realize that he was even a piano player.
Right, later on, yeah.
Yeah, And he really made -- seems as though he made a career out of singing. He was a great, very
great.
Where did this -- this was in Los Angeles?
This was out in Hollywood, this party.
This party in Hollywood, the afternoon -- this party was in the afternoon. Well, were there many people at the party?
Well, not too many. It was mostly musicians. I'd say about up to 15 musicians. And it was great.
Now, did you and Blanton play together at this particular party?
Yeah.
So it was like --
Blanton had his bass and I had mine, and we really --
Two basses? Well, that must have been really great.
It was something else, yeah.
Yeah. Did you find -- how did -- did you find that you and Blanton, in terms of spelling out the harmonic ideas, how did that come out?
We were somewhat alike in our styles, you know, and what I mean is -- it's hard to explain, But I will say that Jimmy, Jimmy Blanton was a wonderful bassist.
And I hope he thought the same thing about myself, you know.
Oh, so you all had a close affinity in terms of the kinds of things that you thought about?
Yes, very close.
Tried to improvise.
Yeah, sure.
Did you do any bow duets?
On, no, no. He did mostly pizzicato, all pizzicato. But he played some wonderful solos, you know, pizzicato, while I stuck to my old bow, you know.
Now, in these sessions did you all tend to play longer solos than, say, on records. I mean like sessions.
Oh, yes, we would play sometimes two and three choruses on different things. We'd play and -- and I can remember playing even one number, 'I've Got Rhythm,' for maybe about an hour or so.
Oh, in that particular session?
Sure.
Oh, that's --
Sure.
Did the piano player switch over on that, I mean like --
Oh, yes, piano, we had piano, and even Nat played a couple of things with the groups, the horn blowers,
Jimmy and myself. I think one fellow, Lee Young, brought his drum set. We had a regular session then, out there.
So like -- when you -- so at that time you and Blanton didn't have any -- you all's stamina was up where you could play for an hour without --
Oh, sure, yes. Yes, youngsters, you know.
(Laughter.)
That must have been quite a sound.

Plucking, and that arm was really flying you know, and being young, of course -- I couldn't do it now quite as much as I did at that time. I still have a little power in my arms and my hands, you know, where I can pluck with, but every once in a while I have to cheat a little bit, you know, yeah.
When you say cheat a little bit, what do you mean?
I mean instead of plucking four time real fast, every once in a while I play two.
Oh, yeah, yeah, I've heard a lot of things played two --
Yeah, sure, instead of that fast 4/4.
Right. Sometimes they play -- guys will play a pedal too, just sit one place and go boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom --
That's right, yeah.
But it's -- stay one place.
(Laughter.)
Sure.
And they say, you all got it, you know.
Sure.
So do you remember who some of the other player -- the horn players were at that particular session?
Well, I think Rex Stewart was on the scene at that party. Oh, let me think. It's -- oh, let's see. This was in the mid-'40s, you know. And --
Actually it was the early '40s, because I think Blanton was dead in '42.
Yeah. Well, it would have to be the early '40s, maybe 1940, yeah.
You see --
I can't think of some of the other musicians. But every once in a while we -- the cats used to get together, and especially after the Lovejoy's, the home of the Big Leg Chicken, you know --
Yeah, right up in there.
And that was the spot.
Now, at these did many people from other -- the other kinds, people like, say, people who were in,

like they owned other kinds of things, did they come to the parties that you all played? Because I know a lot of guys have mentioned a lot of, you know, the stuff that was written about jazz people like George Raft, others were jazz followers coming around. Did they -- when you were in any of the bands that you were in, did you have any people from the movie colony there come to hear you --
Yes.
-- who you got to know?

Yes. I think, if I remember, Slim and I were invited out to Martha Raye's house to a party, and it was -- and George Raft, yeah. They were -- they had parties, you know, I was able to get in on, and it was great.
Now, did you play at those parties?
Oh, yes, sure. Yeah.
Do you remember who all was at the party that you had at Martha Raye's in terms of musicians, the people who came?

Well, it's hard for me to remember offhand right now, but local musicians, yeah, both white and black, you know what I mean. And it was a beautiful scene. I wish I could remember some of the happenings.
What kind of a person is Martha Raye?
Oh, beautiful. She would sing with us, you know, and have a good time.
HEMLOCK
How about George Raft? Did he dance?
Oh, yes. Yeah.
I know he was quite a dancer.
Yes, oh, yes. It was all so beautiful.

I even played quite a few more parties. We were invited to quite a few parties. I can't even remember the names, but it was quite a life, and it was beautiful, yes. That's the reason why I say from time to time I haven't had a chance to run across any prejudice, you know, and what have you. Everybody seemed to be so beautiful, even personally, that is.

I remember when I played down in the Deep South with Slim, there were occasions where we were, Slim and I were invited to some of the folks where we were playing. We were invited to their homes. And there was no sign of prejudice and what have you. They were music lovers, I can imagine, and Slim and I were treated royally, you know.
Oh, yeah, right. Like when you say the Deep South, which places?
Oh, as far as Alabama and through the South, you know.
So like most of the places that you -- most of the places that you played you were -- you would be invited to a private situation --
Oh, yes.
-- which was very different from the
formal kind of public situation.
Oh, yes, yeah.
Do you remember any of the people who invited you to play there at their homes?

Well, not offhand. It's been so long. But that's the way it was. I've never had the chance to even think about the way things actually were, prejudice and what have you. I don't have time to even think about it.
So you didn't -- so you're saying that you hardly ever experienced it?
I hardly ever, you know, hardly ever.
Well, you've had the most unique life of any of the musicians I've interviewed so far.
Yes, right.
Just about everybody that I've talked to, they -- that was a recurrent kind of thing that they had to deal with. It might not be in terms of the jazz audience so much.
Right.
But in terms of what was happening when they were traveling, you know.

Yeah, traveling across -- like when I first mentioned when I went up to Boston, I had noticed some signs of it, you know, but it wasn't enough to make me the least bit concerned over it, because I had so many other
interests, you know, that I didn't even think about it.
Now, when you were -- what kinds of when you were playing in the South? places did you play with the (inaudible)?
Dance halls, you know, theaters. And I think one spot we played in Atlanta in a club, and at that particular time with Slim that was integrated.
Huh!
Sure.
Do you know what year this was?
That was around '40.
It was?
That's right.

Because I remember Sonny Greer told me that, when he played -- they played in Atlanta. They played in Atlanta, played -- the white people were in the gallery. The black people were dancing. The white people were up in the gallery watching, but they weren't dancing.
Yeah, that could have been, but I didn't even notice it. When we played a couple of theaters, I remember we played Baltimore and Washington, of course.
What kind of -- how did Washington strike you as a city in those days?
It was beautiful. Of course, in Washington I might say, if I remember correctly, I didn't -- let's see, I did play Washington once with Slim, and that was
in '40. And it was cool, really.
Uh-huh. Where did you work? Did you work at the Howard Theater?
Howard Theater, right.
You worked at the Howard.
And I didn't -- it was a good scene, but I mean...
Where did you -- where did you -- when you were -- what kind of -- when you were traveling, what kind of living accommodations did you have?
Well, hotels.
Well, did you -- did you live in hotels anywhere in the cities that you wanted to stay in or did you just live (inaudible)?
Well, usually like -- I think there's a Dunbar in Washington also. We stayed there -- and a couple of colored hotels, you know.

Uh-huh. How did the -- how did the -- did you find yourself at that time becoming -- where people would start asking you for autographs and stuff when you'd be on the streets or something, did people begin to recognize you when you walked after a few years with Gailard?
That's right. They were constantly asking us for autographs and what have you.
Whether you were working or you were
walking around --
That's right.

Well, now, when you -- which of the bands that you were working with did you think that you began to get the most attention playing?
Well, I -- when you say "bands," --
Any groups.
Any groups.

Did you prefer working as a side man to being a leader?

Well, I was just as happy working as a side man rather than being a leader because I had found that being a leader is quite a bit of pressure involved and at times, you don't -- you really don't want to go through some of the hassles that are involved sometimes. I have been a

leader, I'd say on a couple of occasions, when I had a couple of groups. It wasn't too bad, but there were times that you have to study the situation real hard in order to get along with your co-workers and what have you, at times, even musically.

Well, I would -- let's see if I can remember. One time, after Billy Taylor was with me for a while on piano, after Billy left, I had a young lady to play piano with me. Her name was Beryl Booker and of course, let's see, I had a quartet at that particular time with Johnny Collins on the guitar and Harold West on the drums and of course, there were times when we -- there were little situations where they used to argue amongst themselves, you know, and I tried to get them straight, cool things and what have you. But at times, there was a bit of responsibility in order to keep harmony in the group.
That was one of the times when I'd rather not have been a leader, you know.
Oh, because of trying to keep the people in the band --
Happiness in the family, you know,
harmony, you might say.
So that's why you chose to not keep leading bands?
That's right, sure.
Now, it was mentioned at one point that -- your wife mentioned that there was a situation when you were with Art Tatum when he was driving a car.
(Laughter.)

Oh, well, yes. This happened to be -- this took place out in Los Angeles. In fact, we -- I was working with Art at the Streets of Paris and of course, a lot of our friends used to come by to see us on the job. This particular time, I want to remember, is if you can remember the singer Al Hibbler --
Right, blind singer.

That's right. He came by one night to see us at the club, Streets of Paris, where we were working, Art Tatum Trio. It was nice to see Al and here's what really happened. Al Hibbler and Art, they used to get in arguments, you know, friendly arguments, of who could do this and who could do that, you know. I imagine they were referring to their being blind and what have you and Art would say he can do things better than Al could do them and vice versa, you know. And this particular night, when Hibbler came in, as we were leaving the club to -- I was driving that night in my car, you know, and

we had asked Al to come with us up to Lovejoy's on this particular night to jam a little while, you know, to a session. So one word led on to another between Al and Art and somehow, they started arguing amongst themself -- I don't know how it started -- they started arguing, friendly-like, about who could drive a car, you know?
(Laughter.)
And this thing went on and Art would say to Al, "Oh, I can drive better than you man. You can't drive no car."
(Laughter.)

And the same, vice versa, Al would holler over to Art that he could drive better than he. In fact, the argument started as we started -- when I started the car to take us all up to the session, you know. They were in the back seat of the car. The guitar player and myself -- I was driving, you know, up front. All this argument was going on and I had just started out -- oh, we were -- hadn't gone a block. Art would holler out, "Stop the car, Slim. Stop the car. I'm going to show this cat who's the better driver," you know. So I don't know what he was getting at. I stopped the car, pulled over and stopped the car, and Art said to Al, "Well, I tell you what, Al. Here's your chance to drive the car because I can drive better than you, I'm sure."
So Al backed down. Al said to Art, "Well, man, you know I can't drive." But anyway, one word led on to another

and Art said, "Well, I can drive." And Al wanted to disprove him. So he said, "Slam, let me get over to the wheel," which I did. Al was in the back seat laughing and Art -- I started the car up for Art and let him get behind the wheel and do you know that Art drove at least a block down the street? Somehow this particular street, he must have known how the situation was, because he kept a straight line right down the street. Fortunately, there wasn't much traffic.
(Laughter.)

He pulled over to the curb after a while and stopped. So that was one of the -- I was so frightened, everybody was, you know. But this was one of the experiences that I never will forget, that Art Tatum actually drove a block down the street.
(Laughter.)
When did you join Benny Goodman's band?
I joined Benny in 1945.
Oh, so this was like after --
I had come back closer to home, you know, New York City. I was working the Three Deuces.
That was when you were working with Tatum, Three Deuces?
Yeah, yeah.
And then -- was this around the time that Tatum got ill and you --
Yeah, this was the time when -- yeah.
So when you weren't working with your own band with Collins and West and Garner, that was when you went into Goodman's sextet.
With Goodman, yes.
Now, who all was in Goodman's sextet when you went in?
