Now, when you were traveling over there, did you play under -- what circumstances did you tend to perform under? Were you playing clubs or concert halls or festivals or all of them?

Concert halls, festivals and on one occasion, we played nightclub. Of course, getting back to the recording part, I had -- was a wonderful feeling -- I had the opportunity to do a recording with Stephane Grapelli. Have you heard that name?
Oh, yeah, the violinist.
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah, I've heard him. He's very -- he's got quite a reputation.
Right. As a matter of fact, John Guarnieri was on that recording at the piano and Jimmy Shirley, whom I mentioned, and Jackie Williams. But that particular
record session, when it came out, I was surprised to note that on the label of the album that we had made, it was called "Stef and Slam."
Oh, you mean -- so are you saying that when you went in the studio with your group. Is that what you mean?
No, that was Stepan's recording date.
That was his session, uh-huh.
That was his.
But then they put --
But they included me on the album cover with Stef as "Steph and Slam."
So you were almost -- you were billed as co-leader kind of.
The same -- yeah.
Right. Did you get paid for being a co-leader or were you paid (inaudible)?
Well, I was paid a little more than side man, you know.

Uh-huh. Yeah, well, you know, sometimes record companies do that, where they'll pay you -- they won't pay you a certain way, then they'll use your name as -- like Coltrane , for instance, made one record where he was the side man. Then when he became very famous, they put the record back out under his name. Didn't give him any more
money.
That's right, yeah.
(Laughter.)
That's what I was trying to find out, if that was what they did in that kind of a situation. Now, you have also, through -- hold on one moment.
(Recording interruption.)

So now, since you've been here in Binghamton, you've also expanded your -- the type of performances that you do to include working not only with the orchestra, in a movie, but you've also performed for -- with string quartets and orchestras.
That's right, yeah.
Now, firstly, I'd like you to talk a bit about the orchestra score that you did. We mentioned it earlier in the first tape, but --

Oh, the orchestra score that I did for a French movie? Yes, this took place in 1976. I went to France to perform this bit of music with the French Symphony. It was supposed to be for a French movie, which I did, and it turned out real well, as far as I was concerned, musically. But then, after I had heard from some source that the movie didn't take so well. So what they had done to this background music for the French movie, they made a recording out of it, which was -- sold quite well, I'm sure, and I have not received
any compensation for this particular recording that they had made. In fact, they didn't give -- they did it without my permission at all.

You mentioned too something this morning about, before we began taping, about a few -- aren't there a few other compositions available on the recording that you did in the studio? Is that the recording? That's not that one.
No, that's not the one.
It's another one.
No.
Now, you were -- well, now, since we're talking about France, --
France, yeah.
Now, you had, you and your wife Claire (PHONETIC) who's here with us, --
Yes.
-- mentioned the fact that there was some other music that you did, that you came up with some tunes in the studio. And what did you say was happening, Claire?

Well, he -- I would say there are probably ten songs that he came up with in the studio that he named and are -- on the record, are given credit as Ogner Bozer (PHONETIC). Now, ASCAP has received a letter that they want to claim the royalties on it.
The producer of the record? The record

Yes, the record company, who is also the producer. It's the same person. And what we have done is to inform ASCAP that all of our rights are, you know, belong to us and informed ASCAP that he would collect his own royalties on his own songs and they're not to be assigned to anybody but Slam Stewart.

Okay, all right. Now you were mentioning too that there is going to be a problem of bootleg recordings taking place at festivals in certain situations. Could you elaborate a bit on that since we're talking about France and Europe?

Yes, that is quite a problem. I remember on two or three occasions when I appeared in France and different parts of Europe, even in Germany, Denmark, Switzerland, where when we were appearing and performing, we'd run across situations where we were being recorded by someone in the audience. Somehow we could detect that they were recording our performance and that's how the bootlegging department has grown through the years. It's really a sad situation, to see the way that has happened.
Yeah, the guys were coming over there to perform and then they're being recorded.
They're being recorded in the -- in an unorthodox way.
HEMLOCK ERASABLE
Now, the company that you're having problems with over your music, is that Black and --
Black and Blue.
Black and Blue.
Black and Blue, that's right.
So they're going to try to live up to their name.
Yes, that's right. They are living up to their name. It's quite a tragedy.
Now, you -- now, here, you have -- could you talk a bit about the work that you were doing with the -- that you did with the string quartets --
Yes, yes.
-- and the harpsicordists and --
Yes.
-- (inaudible).

I've done quite a bit of work with the Lincoln String Quartet of Southern Illinois and the Camarado (PHONETIC) Woodwind Quintet of Western Illinois University and we have done quite a bit of work, especially for the -- sponsored by the National Council on the Arts.
Now, how did this -- how did your involving yourself with those kind of musicians come about?
Yes, well, it so happened that they were invited here to play for an institution called Robeson

Center and so of course, being connected with the Robeson Center here, I had the opportunity to do my bit with them. I was asked to do concerts with them while they were doing a sort of a workshop affair.
It was a music conference.

A music conference. And that's how that started. I had special arrangements written for me and of course, I worked right along with them. You don't usually hear of a bass player playing with a quartet, you know.
Never do, then it's a quintet.

During this happening, I injected my bit of jazz into this department -- of course, normally I played right along with them and of course, in between the different movements, I would play a jazz cadenza, a cadenza leading into the next movement, which might be into a different key even in these pieces that we played and that was quite -- something new that has never been done before.
How did the string quartet react to it?
Oh, my goodness, they really -- Claire, could you tell him about how they reacted?

Well, that was beautiful. He printed that too, when he played with the Indianapolis Symphony. They loved the idea. They took the principals of their orchestra, you know, after he had done his big number with them and they repeated it with the principals of the orchestra and
everyone who's heard it has just flipped over it.
Now, you -- has this been recorded?
No, no.
This hasn't been recorded. Which year did this take place -- which years?
So, three. '70, '71 and '72.
Yeah, right.

Now, it seems to me, when we were talking at breakfast a couple of days ago, which you -- either you or your wife said that the first time you performed for the National Council of the Arts, that there was -- was that the one where you said there was the biggest -- how can I put it?
Most sophisticated audience in the United States.
As far as the music educators and people, in that there was a --
Oh, yes.
How did they respond to it at the first performance, the audience?
The audience was -- oh, my goodness. They stood up in the aisles and everyplace else in the place. Where did we play? We played at --
St. Louis.

St. Louis, yes. They really -- especially, I must say, I did a fairly good job in making them rise, to stand up out of their chairs, you know. In fact, when I came on with my bit in the cadenzas that I would play, and it was a real kick, jazz against this serious string music and what have you.
Who were some of the composers that you -- music that you were performing?
Oh, let's see, Bach, Beethoven --
Haydn.
-- Haydn.
Oh, you did some of those famous Beethoven string quartets, did you?
Yes, yes.
Oh, my, my.
Mozart.
Yeah.
And so they really went
Oh, they enjoyed it so much, yes. You could really see it.
And now you -- and now that was the first year you worked with the string quartet.
That's right, yes.
Now, the second year, did you work with them as well?
Well, I worked with them part of the second year and of course, I also played with the Binghamton Symphony here at home.
Oh, that was the one you talked about in the first tape, where Jack Martin wrote the -- was it when you performed "Play, Fiddle, Play" with the orchestra?
Yes, right.
And did he also write a work --
Yes, an original score.
An original score. What was the name of that?
(Foreign phrase.) La Rêve symphonique pour Slam
What does that mean, now, you're trying to say?
"A Symphonic Dream for Slam."
"A Symphonic Dream for Slam" is what it translates into?
Yeah, right.
Okay. That's Jack Martin did that.
Yes.
How was that received?
That was very well.
That was very well received too, right? And now, the third year for the National Council of the Arts, you worked with students from Boston?
A jazz group.
A jazz group, yes, that's right.
And that was for the same -- so then --
Yes.
So the first year was the string quartet, --
The second year, he worked with a harpsicordist doing the same baroque music. I mean, also baroque, not the same music, but also baroque.
Baroque music, the second year at the National Council.
No, at the music conference at Robeson Center.
Oh, okay, all right. The first year, the music conference at Robeson Center is with the orchestra, the second year was with a harpsicordist.
The first year was Lincoln Center. They took it on tour after the music conference.
Okay, now, let's see. We're getting closer to the last one now.
Yes.

Now, what are your performance intentions at this point? Do you intend to record any of this -- of these kind of things, like the string -- work with the string quartet or the orchestra pieces or baroque music with the harpsicordist or any of those things? Or do you have other
kinds of plans and things that you plan to do (inaudible)?

Well, I -- my main thing at the time that I'm looking forward to is going to Boston to do some things at the Berklee School of Music, for one thing, and -- which I'm very serious about, especially I'm looking forward to playing with the Boston Pops and also many pop orchestras all over the country.
And symphonies.
And symphonies and what have you.
That have taken interest in what you're doing, beginning to --
Yes, right.
What are some of the other pop orchestras and symphonies that are interested in working with you, besides Boston?
San Francisco called him about two months ago.
Yes.
San Francisco Symphony?
For their symphony, yes.
Now, do they intend to do work that's already been written for him, like the Jack Martin piece ?
No. So little was written for bass. They have to rely on what he has.
Oh, so they're going to use some of the scores --
Yeah, right.
Yes, right.
-- that are available.
Now, we have commissioned new scores that are now being written specifically for symphony and pops orchestras.
Now, who's writing the scores?
Right now -- of course, Jack has written the one.
Jack Martin.
Jack Martin, the one. But a young student who is terribly talented named Bobby Frankivello (PHONETIC), he did one symphonic score for Slam when he was 18 that was quite successful and now he's 19.
And he's writing another one?
His writing would scare you. You'd swear he was 59, not 19.
So he's one of the people?
He's doing five new scores for Slam.
He's doing five new scores for Slam in orchestra?
Yes, yes.
And so will this be an orchestra like of
80 pieces of so?
Running from 50 to 80.
Anywhere from 50 up.
That's right.
50 to 80, right.
Okay. And so in closing then, you have been -- you are beginning to be as well received as a bassist in the so-called straight world of music --
That's right, yes.
-- as you have been these many years in the jazz world.
That's for sure, yes.
Well, it looks like we've gotten to the end, Mr. and Mrs. Stewart. And I must say, I think we've got some for them to listen to and some for them to make a film to.
Yes, indeed.
Thank you very much. It's been quite a pleasure.
And thank you, also.
Okay. You got it.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
SLAM STEWART
SLAM REMEMBERS ERROLL GARNER

I treasure my memories of Erroll Garner. . .his endearing elfin grin, his humorous wit and his incredible ability to attain the sound of an entire symphony when he was playing. He was always composing. He would weave intricate harmonies into a simple song until it became an exquisite concerto of memorable beauty. He took great delight in surprising me with rhythmic innovations and I remember fondly how he would look up at me for approval.

During our days on 52nd Street, we used to hang out together at the White Rose Bar with all of the other musicians. . .the drinks were inexpensive and the food was free. While we were playing The Three Deuces, I took my quartet into the Strand Theater with Erroll on piano, Johnny Collins on guitar and Harold West on drums. We played all the theater shows then went on to The Deuces until about two in the morning. After that, Erroll and I joined Art Tatum and we went uptown to Harlem to after-hours spots where we all played some more. The great Tatum had a few favorite pianists and Erroll was one of them. Erroll also had great admiration for Tatum. They would get into a 'cutting' session and would try to outdo one another. Those places were always full of musicians who were anxious to play but not one pianist ever dared to play a note when those two 'Gods' were in the house. The memories I have of the two of them playing are priceless.

Erroll always gave me credit for helping him get in the 'big time' but he would have achieved that anyway. I knew the first time I heard him play that he was a giant! I saw Erroll only occasionally over the years but the love and admiration we felt was always there. He was my brother. The unforgettable sound of Erroll Garner will live forever!
MARTHA GLASER

Dear Friends;

January 2nd, 1981, will mark the fourth anniversary of the death of Erroll Garner.

Memories of him, both as a man and as an artist, continue with an immediacy; his music remains ever present, ever fresh.

From bassist Slam Stewart, who was Erroll's good friend and performing companion, we have another memoir, which we wish to share with you on this occasion.

We join again with friends in remembrance.

Sincerely,

Martha Glaser

521 FIFTH AVENUE
NEW YORK, N.Y. 10017

segments.title: Opening of tape one and interview setup
segments.summary: Header, date and Crouch's opening introduction of the Smithsonian interview with Slam Stewart.

segments.title: Birth in Englewood, only child, violin at seven, big bands on radio
segments.summary: Stewart was born in Englewood, NJ in 1914, an only child raised strictly. His parents bought him a violin at about seven and he listened to Ellington and Lunceford on the radio.

segments.title: Englewood neighborhood, violin teacher Professor Scott, the pull of the bass
segments.summary: He describes the country-like town, his violin teacher Professor Scott, and how the sound of the band bassist drew him from the violin to the bass.

segments.title: Father's work for the Morrow family and their support for his music
segments.summary: His father was a gardener for Dwight Morrow's family; the Morrows helped finance his music study in Boston.

segments.title: Little segregation in Englewood; first noticing it on the way to Boston
segments.summary: Asked about Englewood's mix, Stewart says he noticed no segregation at home but first saw it on the train and in Boston stations and restaurants.

segments.title: High school orchestra: playing bass by ear, switching from violin at fourteen
segments.summary: Looking at a photo of the school orchestra, Stewart says he played bass without reading, was shown how to tune it, and switched from violin at about fourteen.

segments.title: Playing dances with Sonny Marshall and his Harlem Stompers
segments.summary: With a car from his father he traveled to Newark and Passaic to play adult dances in Sonny Marshall's small combo, his first experience in a jazz group.

segments.title: Records and radio; first seeing Ellington at the Apollo with his parents
segments.summary: He learned from radio and a few records, especially Ellington, and remembers his parents taking him to the Apollo where he focused on the bass player.

segments.title: Repertoire and keys with the Marshall band
segments.summary: The group played blues and tunes like Shine and Chinatown, My Chinatown, mostly in C, B flat and F.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Going to Boston after high school, around 1934
segments.summary: Stewart confirms he went to Boston around 1934 after high school, having worked mostly with Marshall's band.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Dean Earl's band at the Little Dixie and Ray Perry's humming violin
segments.summary: In Boston he played in Dean Earl's band at the Little Dixie; alto and violin player Ray Perry, who sang along with his violin, gave him the idea to hum along with his bowed bass.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Early bass influences, the Calloway bassist, and the straight tuba-like bass style
segments.summary: Asked about early models, he recalls a Cab Calloway bassist who twirled his bass, and says bassists then played mostly straight pizzicato with little syncopation.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Studying at the Boston Conservatory with Al Ropes
segments.summary: He studied bow technique, solfeggio and reading with Al Ropes at a small conservatory over Child's Restaurant, learning the bass clef.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Playing by ear in the school orchestra; Margaret Reed; tuning in fourths
segments.summary: He played marches by ear in the school orchestra, his teacher Margaret Reed let him try the school's bass, and he explains bass versus violin tuning.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: School orchestra repertoire and his proud parents
segments.summary: They played Sousa-type marches pizzicato without amplification; his parents came to hear him and were very proud.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Being told he was adopted, strict upbringing, church choir, family support for music
segments.summary: He says he was told he was adopted, was raised strictly, sang baritone in church, and that his family and relatives encouraged his music.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Leaving the Conservatory after half a semester
segments.summary: He studied only half a semester because his family had paid for a half term and he could not afford more; most of his reading came from working.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Joining Peanuts Holland's group in Buffalo and its repertoire, 1935
segments.summary: A bandleader passing through Boston called him to Buffalo, where he joined Peanuts Holland's small group for about six months, playing Ellington-era standards.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Playing the Silver Grill in Buffalo
segments.summary: The band played the Silver Grill restaurant-nightclub, starting about 8:30 and working forty minutes on, twenty off.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Peanuts Holland's trumpet idols and the band's keys and members
segments.summary: Holland admired Armstrong, Rex Stewart, Cootie Williams and Hot Lips Page; Stewart still played by ear in three keys and recalls only altoist Don Stovall.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: A white-owned club with a mixed audience and no racial problems
segments.summary: The Silver Grill was white-owned with a mixed clientele and no problems, which Crouch calls unusual for 1935; Boston was the same.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Leaving Buffalo with the humming-and-bowing style formed
segments.summary: On leaving Buffalo he was already humming and bowing, and again credits Ray Perry as his inspiration.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Building stamina and finger strength on the bass
segments.summary: He built strength by playing long nights and practicing daily to strengthen his hands and fingers.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Left-hand technique: unorthodox two-finger vibrato
segments.summary: Stewart uses the classical position but gets vibrato or tremolo with two fingers, one fixed and one shaking, a style of his own.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Intonation, Blanton, and a good ear
segments.summary: Crouch compares his intonation to Jimmy Blanton's; Stewart credits focused practice, a good ear and strong fingers.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Right-hand technique and the fanning motion on fast tempos
segments.summary: They discuss plucking with two fingers, the fan motion bassists used on fast tunes, and the thumb brace.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Studying harmony and asking musicians to play notes for him
segments.summary: He studied harmony in Boston, then kept learning by having musicians play notes for him and by working out bass lines with pianists.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Simple harmonies in the mid-1930s; deeper harmony came with Art Tatum
segments.summary: His harmonic playing in the mid-'30s was simple; more advanced harmony came later, especially with Tatum.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Bass-player friends in New York: Blanton, Pettiford, Lucas, Hinton, Major Holley
segments.summary: He names Blanton, Oscar Pettiford, Al Lucas, Milt Hinton and Major Holley as bassist friends.

segments.chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
segments.title: Passing tones and the pop tunes that opened up the harmony
segments.summary: Half his work was bowed solos and humming; passing tones replaced plain triads, helped by ballads like The Man I Love and Tenderly.

segments.title: Harlem jam sessions and meeting Slim Gaillard at Jock's
segments.summary: After Buffalo he hunted for jam sessions in Harlem, met Slim Gaillard at Jock's on Seventh Avenue, and was invited onto Slim's WNEW radio program.

segments.title: How Slim and Slam got their name, with Martin Block
segments.summary: After the WNEW broadcast, manager Martin Block backed them as an act; they searched for a name and settled on Slim and Slam in late 1935.

segments.title: Touring theaters and clubs, and the dance routine
segments.summary: Under Block's management they played theaters up the East Coast and in Chicago and clubs like the Southland in Boston, and Slim taught him dance steps for the act.

segments.title: Comedy versus music, and bass solos in the 1930s
segments.summary: Stewart insists he was serious about his music; he was already featured as a bowed and humming soloist before meeting Slim.

segments.title: Bowed bass solos as a novelty; Slim and Slam ends in 1941
segments.summary: Bowing was almost unheard of in jazz bass then; Stewart popularized bowed solos and bassists like John Kirby were fascinated. The duo lasted until Slim was drafted in 1941.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Meeting Jimmy Blanton in Chicago with Ellington, 1939
segments.summary: Stewart met Blanton in Chicago in about 1939 while Slim and Slam were playing there; Crouch recalls Billy Taylor leaving the Ellington band because of Blanton.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Blanton's showmanship, big sound and bowing; Jack the Bear
segments.summary: He praises Blanton's pizzicato, big sound and speed, notes he bowed a little but never sang, and mentions Jack the Bear and his early death.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: What Blanton was like as a person; egotism among musicians
segments.summary: Blanton was pleasant company though perhaps fast-living; Stewart says few musicians were egotistical.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Benny Goodman the taskmaster and his glare
segments.summary: Stewart got along with Goodman by staying out of his way; Goodman was a perfectionist known for the glare.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Blanton's harmonic sophistication and Ellington's writing for bass
segments.summary: They discuss Blanton's notes forming independent melodies in Ellington's writing; the two seldom talked bass but admired each other's style.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Slim and Slam in Los Angeles in 1940-41 and local jam sessions
segments.summary: The duo went to L.A. around 1940, played the Swanee Inn and attended after-hours jam sessions with local musicians.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Slim drafted; Stewart joins Art Tatum in late 1941
segments.summary: After Slim was inducted, Stewart, passed over by the draft, joined Art Tatum in Los Angeles in late 1941, staying on and off for several years.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Tape change: start of cassette 2
segments.summary: End of tape one and opening of cassette 2, with date and location.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Keeping up with Tatum's strange keys and modulations
segments.summary: Tatum worked in unusual keys like A, B and E; Stewart kept up by ear and found Tatum surprised and pleased.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Rehearsals with Tatum and Tiny Grimes
segments.summary: The trio rehearsed often with guitarist Tiny Grimes on a variety of ballads, pop tunes and fast numbers Tatum chose.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Following Tatum's runs and his key-change tricks
segments.summary: Stewart explains how he followed Tatum's fast runs and sudden modulations through an open ear, and says he grew more with Tatum than anyone.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Tiny Grimes struggles; Tatum expects players to know every key
segments.summary: Grimes sometimes laid out when Tatum changed keys; Crouch suggests Tatum wanted anyone who played with him to handle every key.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Who sat in with the Tatum trio
segments.summary: Almost nobody sat in; occasionally horn players such as Don Byas and Roy Eldridge did, but not Charlie Parker.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: First reaction to bebop; recording with Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Stewart went along with bebop and was hired for record sessions with Gillespie and Parker (Hot House), crediting his Tatum experience for his ease with it.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Charlie Parker as a person and his search for new sounds
segments.summary: Parker was friendly; Stewart asked how he developed bebop and thinks Parker was as harmonically impressive as Tatum.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: What Tatum admired: Garner, Fats Waller and Don Lambert
segments.summary: Tatum talked about Garner, Fats Waller and especially the Princeton pianist Don Lambert, whom he loved.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: John Collins replaces Tiny Grimes
segments.summary: Guitarist John Collins joined Tatum and Stewart after Grimes left and worked out much better.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: A week with Coleman Hawkins and Roy Eldridge in Providence
segments.summary: Around 1949, while still with Tatum, Stewart did a week with Hawkins and Eldridge in a Providence club.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Tatum as half improviser, half routine
segments.summary: Tatum's numbers were about three-quarters set routine and one-quarter improvisation, so Stewart could predict much of what he played.

segments.chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
segments.title: Keeping a successful recorded solo; It's Got to Be This or That
segments.summary: Stewart improvised solos differently each time but kept a solo that worked on a hit record, citing It's Got to Be This or That with Goodman.

segments.title: Major Holley takes up the bow and sings with his bass
segments.summary: Few bassists took up the bow after him, but Major Holley, a friend since the late '30s, tried to outdo him, singing in his bass register.

segments.title: 52nd Street and the Three Deuces
segments.summary: Stewart first played 52nd Street with Tatum at the small Three Deuces, which had a well-kept Steinway baby grand and three or four shows a night.

segments.title: Meeting Oscar Pettiford at the White Rose Bar
segments.summary: Stewart met Pettiford on the Street, the two hung out at the White Rose, and he judges Pettiford very good but not quite Blanton.

segments.title: Which bassists had the biggest sound
segments.summary: Walter Page had an immense sound; others named are Hinton, Blanton, Pettiford and Braud.

segments.title: Amplification of the bass in the 1930s and 40s
segments.summary: Some basses used amplifiers like the Ampeg, but Stewart mostly relied on the house system.

segments.title: Hearing Dizzy Gillespie's first bebop band and reacting to bebop
segments.summary: Stewart heard the 1944 band with Pettiford and Don Byas; he found Gillespie's playing a bit way out while Parker was more pleasant, and he did not explain it to others.

segments.title: Drummers he played with and his own quartet with Garner, West and Collins
segments.summary: He played with Jo Jones and Sid Catlett, and led his own quartet with Erroll Garner, drummer Harold West and John Collins while Tatum was away.

segments.title: Discovering Erroll Garner at Tondelayo's and giving him his first group job
segments.summary: When Tatum went home ill, Stewart hired Garner, whom he found at Tondelayo's on 52nd Street, for the Three Deuces; Garner credited him with his first professional group gig.

segments.title: Garner versus Tatum as accompanists for his solos
segments.summary: Garner improvised and accompanied Stewart's solos with room to breathe, while Tatum tended to play all over the piano.

segments.title: Tape change within cassette 2
segments.summary: Crouch ends side A as the tape runs out.

segments.title: Art Tatum the pinochle player
segments.summary: Tatum loved pinochle and held cards close to his good eye; Stewart and guitarists played with him for fun.

segments.title: Tatum, football and musicians' interest in sports
segments.summary: Tatum was said to have been hurt playing football and loved it; they talk about Black football and baseball teams and band baseball games.

segments.title: Interests outside music, Garner, and going to the movies
segments.summary: Stewart was wrapped up in music, liked cards, and Garner was similar; he went to movies until TV came.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Making Hellzapoppin with Slim Gaillard
segments.summary: Slim and Slam made Hellzapoppin through the William Morris agency in L.A.; Stewart was paid about $750 and met Olsen and Johnson and Martha Raye.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Appearing in Stormy Weather with Fats Waller
segments.summary: Stewart played in the Fats Waller sequence of Stormy Weather, his only time playing with Waller, whom he found comical and wonderful.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Impressions of the movie business, Lena Horne and Bill Robinson
segments.summary: He was pleased to be in the film, paid about as for Hellzapoppin, and found Lena Horne and Bill Robinson down to earth.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Sitting in with Benny Carter in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Stewart sat in on after-hours sessions with Benny Carter, who lived in L.A., while out there with Slim.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Los Angeles clubs without segregation
segments.summary: Asked about L.A.'s segregated scene, Stewart says the Streets of Paris, 331 Club and Swanee Inn were mixed and he saw no problems.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Where he lived in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Besides hotels, he rented a bungalow on 41st Street near Central Avenue while in town.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Central Avenue and Lovejoy's after-hours spot
segments.summary: Club Alabam was the main Central Avenue club; musicians such as Tatum, Grimes and Stewart went after work to Lovejoy's, near the Dunbar Hotel.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Meeting Lester Young in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Stewart met Lester Young at a session; he found him reserved rather than eccentric, and met his brother Lee Young.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Lester Young's mellow style and harmony
segments.summary: Stewart liked Young's mellow sound and passing changes, so different from Hawkins, and never found his style off-putting.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: First hearing Lester Young; the size of his sound; improvisation
segments.summary: He knew Young from records and Basie; he thinks Young had a big sound, if less than Hawkins, Webster or Chu Berry, and improvised rather than relying on pet phrases.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: A star-studded session and the party where Nat King Cole sang
segments.summary: At a session with Tatum, Barksdale, Ray Nance and Blanton, and at Mary Wilkinson's Hollywood party, Stewart first heard Nat King Cole sing.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Playing two basses with Jimmy Blanton
segments.summary: At the party Blanton and Stewart played together with similar styles; Blanton played only pizzicato while Stewart used the bow.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Hour-long jam sessions, stamina and cheating on fast tempos
segments.summary: They played one tune like I've Got Rhythm for an hour, with Nat Cole and Lee Young; Stewart now sometimes plays in two to save his arm.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Hollywood parties at Martha Raye's and George Raft
segments.summary: Slim and Stewart were invited to movie-colony parties, played at Martha Raye's, and met George Raft.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Rarely meeting prejudice; private invitations in the Deep South
segments.summary: Stewart says he almost never ran into prejudice and was invited into white homes in Alabama; Crouch calls his life unique.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Playing the South, Atlanta and Washington's Howard Theater in 1940
segments.summary: Slim and Slam played dance halls and theaters in the South, an integrated Atlanta club, Baltimore and the Howard Theater in Washington in 1940.

segments.chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Hotels and fans asking for autographs
segments.summary: On tour they stayed in hotels like the Dunbar and were constantly asked for autographs.

segments.title: Tape change: start of cassette 3, January 17
segments.summary: Header and opening of cassette 3, recorded at Stewart's Binghamton home.

segments.title: Where he got the most recognition; preferring sideman work to leading
segments.summary: Stewart names Tatum, Slim Gaillard, the Goodman sextet and his own Garner quartet; he disliked leading because of friction in his quartet with Beryl Booker, Collins and West.

segments.title: The night Art Tatum drove a car in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Tatum and Al Hibbler argued about who could drive; Stewart let Tatum steer a block down the street outside the Streets of Paris, frightening everyone.

segments.title: Joining Benny Goodman's sextet in 1945 through Seven Lively Arts
segments.summary: Goodman heard Stewart at the Three Deuces and asked him to fill in for his brother in the sextet at Seven Lively Arts; Stewart then joined him steadily.

segments.title: Goodman as perfectionist, as improviser, and Artie Shaw's tone
segments.summary: Goodman was a perfectionist with a glare; Stewart thinks he was not the King of Swing and preferred Artie Shaw's tone and harmony.

segments.title: Sitting in with Barney Bigard; not playing with Fats Navarro
segments.summary: He sat in with Bigard, and was not with Goodman when Fats Navarro briefly played with him.

segments.title: Drinking and dissipation among musicians
segments.summary: Stewart on musicians' excess, groove juice, Tatum's heavy drinking that did not affect his playing, and Garner being cooler.

segments.title: Women, integration and Storyville
segments.summary: They discuss women's interest in musicians and how jazz promoted mixing, including Boston's Storyville, where Stewart worked with Tatum.

segments.title: First trip to Europe as first recalled, with Norman Granz
segments.summary: Stewart first places his European debut in the mid-'50s on a Granz package with Erroll Garner, and says he was treated royally.

segments.title: Classical bassists and Koussevitzky's praise
segments.summary: He met no classical bassists in England or during the Tatum years, but Koussevitzky, whom he met briefly in Boston, thought him among the best in jazz around 1938.

segments.title: Concerto-style scores for symphony orchestras
segments.summary: A Binghamton friend wrote scores featuring the bass; Stewart performed with the Binghamton and Indianapolis symphonies.

segments.title: Play, Fiddle, Play and the squeak D with the Binghamton Symphony
segments.summary: In his cadenza Stewart climbs the top string past the violin's top note; Crouch recalls Hank Jones giving up at the top of the piano in a 1976 duo.

segments.title: How he extended the bass range, working on it since 1937
segments.summary: He began developing high notes around 1937, inspired by Ray Perry's violin, and keeps the method secret; he adds comedy at the end.

segments.title: Arvell Shaw's high playing; first recording Play, Fiddle, Play
segments.summary: Crouch compares Arvell Shaw; Stewart says he first recorded Play, Fiddle, Play around 1943 with Garner, for Commodore or another label.

segments.title: Playing Play, Fiddle, Play and the conventional highest bass notes
segments.summary: After an on-tape performance, Stewart says conventional bass stopped near G because higher sounds like a cello, so the high notes were his gimmick.

segments.title: Plucking seven notes with four plucks, and fast tempos
segments.summary: On tape he plays a run where open strings and left-hand hits make seven notes from four plucks, and shows tempos like I've Got Rhythm.

segments.title: Right-hand fingering and the two-finger tremolo demonstrated
segments.summary: He shows plucking with both fingers or one finger braced on the thumb, and the tremolo with first and second fingers on Tenderly.

segments.title: Stardust with and without humming
segments.summary: On tape he plays a Stardust phrase alternately with and without singing, saying humming makes it easier.

segments.title: Using several fingers for a strong low note on gut strings
segments.summary: With high action and gut strings he stacks three fingers behind the note for strength, both arco and pizzicato.

segments.title: High action among the great bassists
segments.summary: Stewart always played with high action; he recalls that Braud, Blanton, Pettiford and Page did too, giving a big sound.

segments.title: Meeting young Charles Mingus in Los Angeles in 1939
segments.summary: Stewart met teenage Mingus at an L.A. club, admired his plucked solos with several fingers and double stops, though they hardly talked.

segments.title: Mingus helping with his bass at a Yale Ellington tribute
segments.summary: At a Yale concert for Ellington, Mingus ran over to help unload Stewart's bass, recalling that Stewart once showed him how to load one in a car.

segments.title: Carrying a bass by car and plane
segments.summary: Stewart describes loading the bass head-first into the back seat, and buying a half-fare seat after flights broke the neck.

segments.title: Playing in groups of several basses; the Pat Boone Show
segments.summary: His only multi-bass work was a late-1950s Pat Boone Show appearance with several bassists.

segments.title: Correcting the first Europe trip: Paris festival in 1948 with Panassie
segments.summary: Stewart realizes his first European trip was the 1948 Paris festival organized by Panassie, with Garner, Bechet, Parker and Miles Davis, before the later England trip.

segments.title: Django Reinhardt and whether they met
segments.summary: He thinks he met Reinhardt in 1948 but never played with him.

segments.title: Playing with Charlie Christian at Timme Rosenkrantz's apartment
segments.summary: Stewart played a couple of sessions with Charlie Christian at Rosenkrantz's 52nd Street pad and found him down to earth and a beautiful player.

segments.title: Minton's Playhouse sessions and keeping up with the new chords
segments.summary: He often went to Minton's where Monk, Clarke and Dizzy worked out bebop; Crouch describes cutting sessions, and Stewart says his ear saved him.

segments.title: Kenny Clarke's drumming and the shift to ride cymbal timekeeping
segments.summary: Stewart accepted Clarke's off-beat accents, and they agree the move from bass-drum quarter notes to ride cymbal let the bassist be heard, which suited Stewart for bebop.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Freelancing after Europe and joining Rose Murphy
segments.summary: He hardly played with Parker and Gillespie beyond one record date; after 1948 he freelanced and worked about a year with pianist-singer Rose Murphy, including a trip to Australia.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Tape change: start of cassette 4, January 18
segments.summary: Header and equipment check opening the last cassette.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Touring with Rose Murphy, the Chi-Chi girl
segments.summary: Murphy sang in a very high voice; they toured the country as a duo and with a drummer, and made an album, for about two years from the mid-'50s.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Touring Australia and its rugby league clubs
segments.summary: In Australia they played rugby league clubs between Sydney and Melbourne, sat in with local musicians, and saw koalas and kangaroos.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Chronology of the early 1950s: his own groups and the Goodman years
segments.summary: Crouch reconstructs the sequence; between 1948 and 1955 Stewart freelanced and led groups with Billy Taylor, Beryl Booker and John Collins, after about two and a half years with Goodman from 1945.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: The war years: 52nd Street and musicians talking about the war
segments.summary: Stewart remembers 52nd Street and the whole country hungry for jazz in 1941-45; musicians discussed the war and Slim was drafted.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Irony of Black musicians being drafted for a segregated country
segments.summary: Crouch asks about the irony of Black musicians fighting without full rights; Stewart says it was seldom discussed and calls the war sad.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Cafe Society opening in 1938 as the first integrated New York club
segments.summary: Stewart was about to leave for the Coast in 1938; Crouch relays Barney Josephson's account that other clubs admitted Black musicians but not Black patrons.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Working at Cafe Society with Tatum; Barney Josephson
segments.summary: Stewart worked there twice with Tatum without feeling bothered, remembers Josephson as a nice person, and Crouch says its success opened 52nd Street clubs.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: The 1945 Town Hall concert and the Indiana duet with Don Byas
segments.summary: At Town Hall promoter Timmie Rosenkrantz asked Stewart and Don Byas to open the second half as a duo with no rhythm section; they played about twelve choruses of Indiana.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Secretly recorded by Rosenkrantz and never paid royalties
segments.summary: The audience cheered, then Rosenkrantz revealed he had taped them; the Commodore release was a big seller but they got no royalties.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: The duet's place in jazz history; first bass and saxophone duo
segments.summary: Crouch calls it one of the great jazz duets; Stewart had never seen a saxophone and bass play alone and was nervous without accompaniment.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Don Byas: advanced harmony, small stature and scraps
segments.summary: Byas sat in with Tatum and played Minton's; Stewart describes him as short but powerful, half humble and half cocky, who got into fights.

segments.chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
segments.title: Tension between servicemen and musicians at the White Rose Bar
segments.summary: Crouch notes the dangerous area near 50th Street; Stewart saw sailors resent musicians out of uniform, causing scuffles.

segments.title: An hour-long duo jam with Roy Eldridge
segments.summary: Eldridge sat in with Tatum, and one night he and Stewart jammed as a duo for an hour in an uptown after-hours place.

segments.title: Trumpeters with harmonic sophistication
segments.summary: He names Eldridge, Joe Newman, Dizzy, Hot Lips Page (the preacher on a recording), Buck Clayton, Shavers and Red Allen.

segments.title: Meeting Louis Armstrong at the Earle Theater; biggest trumpet sounds
segments.summary: Stewart first met Armstrong in 1938 on a Philadelphia bill and thinks Armstrong had the greatest trumpet sound, above Hot Lips Page, Red Allen and Eldridge.

segments.title: Duke Ellington at the Apollo: asked off the bill, later congratulating Slim and Slam
segments.summary: Slim and Slam's first theater job was a bill with Ellington, who had them dropped as too weak; a year later they topped the Apollo bill and Ellington congratulated them.

segments.title: Tape change within cassette 4
segments.summary: Crouch notes the end of side A and the last stretch of the interview.

segments.title: Recording for Harry Lim and 300-400 sides in the 1940s
segments.summary: Stewart recorded often for Harry Lim, including sessions with Johnny Guarnieri, and estimates hundreds of sides with Tatum, Goodman, Parker, Gillespie and others.

segments.title: Recording business, royalties, and Flat Foot Floogie
segments.summary: Stewart says recordings were not much of a rip-off in his time and that royalties on Flat Foot Floogie were his best; Crouch sees it anticipating Louis Jordan.

segments.title: Others borrowing his solos: Goodman record, Johnny Long, Ella Fitzgerald
segments.summary: He recalls his tag on It's Got to Be This or That, Johnny Long arranging his Shantytown solo without paying him, and Ella quoting his Lady Be Good solo as a compliment.

segments.title: The night Big Sid Catlett died backstage in Chicago
segments.summary: While Stewart was with Tatum at a Chicago theater, Catlett visited backstage in good spirits and collapsed with a stroke during the show.

segments.title: Accompanying Billie Holiday in Holiday on Broadway
segments.summary: Stewart's trio with Billy Taylor accompanied Holiday in a mid-'40s Broadway show; he found her reserved, in good shape, and sees Lester Young's influence.

segments.title: Musicians and the civil rights movement
segments.summary: Musicians sometimes talked about Little Rock and the sit-ins; Stewart says he was too wrapped up in music to think much about it.

segments.title: Moving to Binghamton in 1969 and marrying his wife
segments.summary: After freelancing through the 1960s he moved to Binghamton in 1969 to marry a pianist he first met in California while with Tatum.

segments.title: Working with Thelonious Monk at Newport in 1964
segments.summary: His one time with Monk was a festival jam set at Newport in 1964, where Monk played his own modern ideas.

segments.title: Faculty position at Binghamton State University
segments.summary: From 1969-70 he has been part-time faculty, bringing jazz musicians for concerts and workshops.

segments.title: European tours and recordings with Milt Buckner, Jo Jones and others
segments.summary: He toured England, Spain, Italy and Germany with Buckner and Jones, and recorded since 1972 with Big Joe Turner, Wild Bill Davis, Al Casey and others.

segments.title: Recording with Stephane Grappelli, billed as Stef and Slam
segments.summary: In Europe he played concerts and festivals and recorded with Grappelli; the album was billed Stef and Slam and he was paid slightly more than a sideman.

segments.title: Scoring a French film in 1976 and an unpaid recording
segments.summary: He performed a score with the French Symphony in 1976 for a film that flopped; the music was released as a record without his permission or pay.

segments.title: Tunes from a studio session credited to someone else; ASCAP
segments.summary: Claire Stewart explains that about ten tunes he improvised in the studio were credited to another name, and they told ASCAP the royalties belong to Slam.

segments.title: Bootleg recordings at European concerts and the Black and Blue label
segments.summary: Stewart complains about audience members taping performances in Europe and says his problems are with Black and Blue.

segments.title: Playing jazz cadenzas with string quartets and a woodwind quintet
segments.summary: With the Lincoln String Quartet and a woodwind quintet at the Robeson Center music conference he played classical works with jazz cadenzas between movements, 1970-72.

segments.title: The National Council on the Arts audience in St. Louis
segments.summary: The most sophisticated audience of music educators gave a standing reaction to Stewart's cadenzas against Bach, Beethoven, Haydn and Mozart.

segments.title: Binghamton Symphony, Jack Martin's score, and the yearly projects
segments.summary: He played with the Binghamton Symphony, premiered Jack Martin's A Symphonic Dream for Slam, and the wives sort out the baroque, harpsichord and jazz-group projects.

segments.title: Future plans: Berklee, Boston Pops, and new orchestral scores
segments.summary: Stewart plans Berklee and Boston Pops dates, San Francisco has called, and young composers are writing five new scores for orchestras of 50 to 80.

segments.title: Closing of the interview
segments.summary: Crouch says he is received as well in the straight world as in jazz, thanks the Stewarts and ends the recording.

segments.title: Slam's printed memoir of Erroll Garner
segments.summary: An appended piece in which Stewart remembers Garner on 52nd Street, the Strand Theater quartet, after-hours cutting sessions with Tatum, and calls him a brother.

segments.title: Publicist's cover letter for the Garner memoir
segments.summary: Martha Glaser's note marking the anniversary of Garner's death and sharing Stewart's memoir.
